newsitem.title: USA: Jordanian hits Congress vote on Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian hits Congress vote on Jerusalem.

text.p: Jordan Crown Prince Hassan on Monday criticised a U.S. Congress vote reaffirming that Jerusalem should remain Israel's "undivided" capital.
Beginning a visit to Washington, he also stressed the importance of viewing Middle East security from a regional approach rather than what he said was the perspective of "oil, security and Israel."
Hassan, who is expected to meet Tuesday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and later with President Clinton, spoke at the Washington Institute for Near East Peace.

The Clinton administration plans to thank Jordan for its role in the peace process with $100 million in foreign aid drawn equally from the U.S. aid now sent to Israel and Egypt, the Washington Post reported in Tuesday editions, quoting administration officials.
Jordan had its U.S. aid revoked by Congress following its tilt toward Iraq during the Gulf War, and the aid represents the most significant infusion of U.S. help since then.

At least twice in his address, Hassan said that having Congress make pronouncements on the status of Jerusalem "is not helpful at this time" when Israel and the Palestinians are struggling to revive their stalled peace efforts.
Palestinians described as a declaration of war last week's non-binding U.S. House of Representatives resolution calling on Clinton to reaffirm that Jerusalem must remain Israel's "undivided capital."

Israel, which captured Arab East Jerusalem in 1967 and annexed it in a move unrecognized by other nations, including the United States, expressed satisfaction at Tuesday's 406-17 vote in favour of the Sense of Congress resolution.

The vote, which does not oblige the Clinton administration to act, came as Egypt struggled to resolve a peacemaking crisis between Israel and the PLO spurred by Israel's beginning work in March on a 6,500-home Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

In October 1995, the U.S. Senate and the House passed the Jerusalem Embassy Act that states as a matter of U.S. policy that Jerusalem should remain "the undivided capital of Israel" and that the U.S. embassy should be moved there by May 1999.
But, recognising the volatility of the issue of Jerusalem, it allowed Clinton to suspend the embassy's move from Tel Aviv for six-month periods.

In an effort to play down any ill effects of the congressional action, the State Department reiterated its position that it was important the United States not take pre-emptive measures or unilateral measures that might complicate isues pertaining to Jerusalem.
The fate of Jerusalem is supposed to be decided in final status negotiaiotns between Israel and the Palestinains.
Hassan was ominous about the state of peace negotiations saying "I don't think time is on our side."
"The standoff (between Israelis and Palestinians) is dangerous and threatening ... and may lead to the collapse of our (peace) efforts," he said.
